newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.

text.p: CHANCES OF SURVIVAL FADING FOR THOSE BURIED UNDER RUBBLE
Police say the chances of anyone surviving the collapse of two ski lodges at Thredbo, in the Snowy Mountains are fading by the hour.
Electronic sensing equipment has failed to detect any signs of life from about 20 people believed to be buried under the rubble.
Graham Field from the Thredbo ambulance service says rescue efforts may have to be temporarily halted, while a section of the landslide is stabilised.
Mr Field said weather conditions at the resort town are favourable for the rescue operation.
Meanwhile, the Institution of Engineers has called for a risk assessment to be made of the entire village, following the landslip and collapse.
Chair of the Geomechanics Panel, Professor John Carter, said authorities need to ensure that whatever risks exist are tolerable.
Professor Carter, who practices as a geo-technical engineer, said excessive water may have caused the landslip.
He said from information he has been given, it hasn't rained in the area for days.
"It still doesn't rule out water as a possible cause. I guess there's snow in the higher slopes and that's melting and flowing down both over the ground and through the soil," he said.
ACCESS TO TRAPPED LANDSLIP VICTIMS MAY TAKE UP TO TWO DAYS
The Regional Police Commander for Thredbo, Inspector Bruce Johnson says it may take up to two days to get to those trapped under the rubble of the two ski lodges buried by the overnight landslide.
It's feared up to 20 people were in the lodges.
Inspector Johnson has told a news conference the longer it takes the less chance there will be of finding survivors.
But he says authorities have little option but to take the rescue operations slowly, because it's such a delicate operation.
"What we're trying to avoid is any further slippage," Inspector Johnson said.

"Now that's the estimate at this stage. We may lift some of the heavy slabs away and be able to get in a lot quicker. The estimate may itself be a little bit short. I'm afraid I can't really answer that question until we start to really get into it," he said.
The New South Wales Fire Brigade says rescuers are now clearing the sides of the landslip area and should start penetrating into the collapsed structures shortly.
Spokesman Ian Krimmer says a hundred Fire Service personnel from New South Wales and the ACT are among the rescue teams working on the site.
He says they're all specialist trained experts in search and rescue techniques for collapsed structural emergencies.
Mr Krimmer says the fire brigade has provided a huge amount of equipment for the rescue effort, including six thermal imaging cameras that can detect body heat amidst the rubble.

"We have two seismic listening devices, diamond tipped concrete cutting saws, lighting units, air cylinders, hydraulic-lifting equipment. All this technical support is being provided by the Fire Service and it's being used by teams of emergency workers consisting of fire brigade, police, ambulance, SES and other emergency workers," he said.
HIGH COURT DECISION ON STOLEN GENERATION
The High Court has today ruled out an attempt by nine Northern Territory Aborigines to sue the Government for compensation, over the past practice of removing indigenous children from their families.
The group, including stolen children and their parents, argued the Commonwealth Aboriginal Ordinance, under which the children were removed, was constitutionally invalid.
They said it breached the requirement that all people be treated equally and only the courts could order the removal of people.
One of the Aboriginal people involved, Barbara Cummings, said the group has already filed more writs claiming the government breached its duty of care, and the fight will continue.

"We're not going to stop, we're going to keep going, we need to keep going for justice for us, to make peace with ourselves, to make peace with ourpeople, and to make peace with the government," she said.
Acting Prime Minister, Peter Costello, said the Government will abide by the High Court's decision.
MAN CHARGED OVER MURDER OF MOE TODDLER APPEARS IN COURT
The man charged with murdering 14 month-old Jaiyden Leskie at Moe in eastern Victoria, has made a second appearance in the Melbourne Magistrates Court.
28 year-old Greg Domaszweicz has been remanded in custody until the end of November.
The court was filled with Mr Domaszweicz's family and friends and he acknowlegded them during the hearing.
Magistrate, Julian Fitz-Gerald remanded Mr Domaszweicz in custody until November the 27th for a commital mention.

Magistrate Fitz-Gerald told the court that as forensic material is going to be very important to the case, the prosecution must make that evidence available to Mr Domaszeicz's barrister by October the 30th.
A bail application has been lodged in the Supreme Court and is expected to be heard within the next week.
NEED FOR YESTERDAY'S RATE CUT HIGHLIGHTED BY RETAIL DATA
The need for yesterday's cut in official interest rates has been highlighted by the latest retail figures.
Retail sales fell by a seasonally adjusted 1.8 per cent in June.
The fall comes after an improvement in May preceded by a decline in April.

As an indication of the recent stagnation of the retail sector, Bureau of Statistics figures show sales in the three months to June dropped half a per cent lower than for the previous quarter and were only 1.7 per cent higher than for the corresponding period last year.
Big falls in department store and clothing purchases accounted for most of the drop.
The Reserve Bank and the federal government will be counting on the two recent interest rate cuts to improve consumer confidence.
